newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian bus operators to join truck strike.
newsitem.headline: Indian bus operators to join truck strike.

text.p: Nearly 15,000 bus operators in the Indian capital will join a nationwide strike by truck operators, which entered its fifth day on Saturday, crippling trade and pushing up prices.
The Indian Association of Tour Operators (IATO), an association of private local bus operators in New Delhi, said in a statement it will observe the strike on Monday.
"We are forced to take this decision for the first time," the statement said.
"We are already paying several taxes including luxury tax, expenditure tax and road tax," it said. "Now the imposition of more taxes is discriminatory and against all canons of natural justice."

Truck owners launched the indefinite strike on Tuesday in protest against a proposed service tax and a sharp rise in insurance premiums. It has kept some 2.2 million trucks off the roads and paralysed the movement of goods and services.

The strike entered its fifth day as the government and truck owners remained at loggerheads. "The strike is still on," said S.P. Singh, spokesman for the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC). "No solution has been found."
The AIMTC objects to a five percent service tax on road transport which Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed in the federal budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year.
It also opposes a decision by state-owned insurance companies which the transport congress said would raise insurance premiums by between 300 and 400 percent.
"The strike will completely cripple the entire foreign trade of the country, which accounts for nearly $200 million per day," the Bombay-based Western India Shippers' Association said in a statement.
Industry officials said on Friday shortages had pushed up prices of essential commodities such as rice, wheat and edible oil.

The government has ordered states to invoke the Essential Services Act, which empowers authorities to declare the movement of goods an essential service and take punitive action against those blocking it.
"We have also advised the state governments to use their own vehicles and also take the army's assistance for movement of goods," a Surface Transport Ministry spokesman told Reuters.
There were no reports of violence. "We have always advised our members to remain peaceful and not to be provoked and not prevent any vehicle from carrying goods," Singh said.
The AIMTC represents owners of about two million heavy trucks, one million light and medium-weight trucks and 60,000 booking and delivery companies. Truckers move almost two thirds of India's goods.

The government and truck owners have not held talks for several days. "We have been awaiting the government's response to our demands," Singh said. "We want to resolve it, but it is up to the government. The ball is in their court."
